en: Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the monks.

Monks, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, claims his noble and pre-eminent place, turns the Brahma-wheel, and rightly roars the lion’s roar in the assembly.
What are the ten?

DbSū(1) 1. Here, the Tathāgata understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible. That the Tathāgata understands what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible—this is the first power of the Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, [is so called].
He claims the noble, preeminent place of the bull; he turns the Brahma-wheel and rightly roars the lion’s roar in the assembly.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the undertakings of actions and dharmas of the past, future, and present, according to their basis, their cause, their object, and their maturation.

That the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the undertakings of actions and dharmas of the past, future, and present, according to their basis, their cause, their object, and their maturation—[this is the second power].
This is the second power of a Tathāgata, by which power [he acts] as previously described.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the defilement, purification, establishment, and cleansing of the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
This is the third power of a Tathāgata, by which power [he acts] as previously described.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the superior and inferior faculties of other beings;
that the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the superior and inferior faculties of other beings—
this is the fourth power of a Tathāgata, by which power, as previously described, he rightly roars the lion’s roar in the assembly.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the various inclinations of other beings and other individuals;

that the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the various inclinations of other beings and other individuals— this is the fifth power of the Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, [is so called].
He claims the noble, preeminent position of the bull; he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel and rightly roars the lion’s roar in the assembly.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, that the world consists of various elements and many elements.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, that the world consists of various elements and many elements—
this is the sixth power of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, claims his noble and preeminent place and turns the Brahma-wheel.
He roars the true lion’s roar in the assembly.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the path leading to all destinations;
that the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the path leading to all destinations [is the second power].

This is the seventh power of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, claims the noble position of the bull, turns the Brahma-wheel, and roars the perfect lion’s roar in the assembly.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold former abodes, namely: one [birth]... [and so on].

Furthermore, [he recollects] two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many hundreds of births, many thousands of births,
many hundreds of thousands of births, even an eon of dissolution and an eon of evolution.

He recollects even a single aeon of dissolution, many aeons of dissolution, many aeons of evolution, and many aeons of both dissolution and evolution; he remembers: "In that place, those beings were named such-and-such; there I was, with such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a long life and such a duration of stay."

Thus, with its specific characteristics, its causes, and its details, he recollects his manifold previous existences: "This was the limit of my lifespan; having passed away from there, I was reborn there; having passed away from there, I was reborn there; and having passed away from there as well, I was reborn here. Thus he recollects his various former abodes.
That the Tathāgata recollects his manifold previous existences— namely, one birth, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty,
a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, and even many hundreds of thousands of births.
He recollects hundreds of thousands of births— indeed, a *saṃvarta-kalpa*, a *vivarta-kalpa*, a *saṃvarta-vivarta-kalpa*,

many *saṃvarta-kalpas*, many *vivarta-kalpas*, and many *saṃvarta-vivarta-kalpas*— recollecting: "In such-and-such a place, those venerable beings were named thus, and I was there with such a name, of such a birth, and of such a clan."

"Thus did I eat, thus did I experience pleasure and pain, thus was my lifespan long, thus was my duration of stay, thus was the limit of my life; passing away from there, I was reborn there, and passing away from there as well, I was reborn here"— in this way,
he recollects his manifold previous existences with their modes, causes, and details.
This is the eighth power of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, claims his noble and preeminent place, turns the Brahma-wheel,
and rightly roars the lion’s roar in the assembly.
Furthermore, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata [beholds] sentient beings...
He sees beings passing away and being reborn— whether beautiful or ugly, lowly or exalted—
and he understands, as it truly is, how beings fare according to their karma:
that these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct of body, and possessed of misconduct of speech and mind.

Those who revile the noble ones, who hold wrong views, and because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on wrong views— for that cause and with that condition— after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in the hells. Or again, these beings, friends, are endowed with good conduct of body, and endowed with good conduct of speech and mind.

Those who do not revile the noble ones, who possess right view, and who, because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on right view, for that cause and by that condition, are reborn among the gods in a happy destination, in the heavenly world, after the breaking up of the body—
this is what the Tathāgata sees with his purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, as beings are passing away.

He understands, as it truly is, beings passing away and being reborn— whether beautiful or ugly, lowly or exalted, going to a happy destination or a miserable destination— as they arrive according to their karma:
"These worthy beings were possessed of misconduct of body, and possessed of misconduct of speech and mind..."

Those who revile the noble ones, who hold wrong views, and who, because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on wrong views, for that cause and by that condition, are reborn after the breaking up of the body, after death, in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a downfall, in the hells;
whereas these other beings, sirs, are endowed with good conduct of body, and endowed with good conduct of speech and mind.

Not reviling the noble ones, possessing right view, and because of undertaking the karma and dharma of right view— due to that cause and due to that condition— they, upon the breakup of the body, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods.
This is the ninth power of the Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, [is so called].
He claims the noble, bull-like station; he turns the Brahma-wheel and roars the perfect lion’s roar in the assembly.

9. Furthermore, the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the outflows, having realized for himself in this very life the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having attained them and entered into them, proclaims: "Birth is exhausted for me."
"The holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been accomplished; I know there is no further state of being beyond this.

Because the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the outflows, has realized for himself in this very life the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having attained and entered into them, he declares: 'Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived.'"
"What was to be done has been done; I know of no further state of existence.

This is the tenth power of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, claims his noble and preeminent place, turns the Brahma-wheel, and roars the perfect lion’s roar in the assembly. 10.
The Blessed One said this; and those monks, their minds satisfied, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
The Daśabala-sūtra is completed.

*Daśabalasūtra*: DbSū(2) = Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* Sūtra 348 (T 99, II 98a13–b5). Based on the edition by Ernst Waldschmidt. [The Buddha said: “Monks, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata. What ten? Here, monks, a Tathāgata knows as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. This, monks, is the first power of a Tathāgata. Because he possesses this power, he claims his place in the assembly, roars the lion’s roar, and turns the wheel of Brahmā, which has not been turned by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone else in the world. “Furthermore, monks, a Tathāgata knows as it really is the ripening of karmic actions performed in the past, present, and future, according to their causes and conditions. This, monks, is the second power of a Tathāgata. Because he possesses this power, he claims his place in the assembly, roars the lion’s roar, and turns the wheel of Brahmā... “Furthermore, monks, a Tathāgata knows as it really is the various elements of the world with their many and diverse elements. This, monks, is the third power of a Tathāgata. Because he possesses this power, he claims his place in the assembly, roars the lion’s roar, and turns the wheel of Brahmā... “Furthermore, monks, a Tathāgata knows as it really is the various inclinations of beings with their many and diverse inclinations. This, monks, is the fourth power of a Tathāgata. Because he possesses this power, he claims his place in the assembly, roars the lion’s roar, and turns the wheel of Brahmā... “Furthermore, monks, a Tathāgata knows as it really is the faculties of other beings and individuals, whether dull or sharp, superior or inferior, and so forth. This, monks, is the fifth power of a Tathāgata. Because he possesses this power, he claims his place in the assembly, roars the lion’s roar, and turns the wheel of Brahmā... “Furthermore, monks, a Tathāgata knows as it really is the way leading to all destinations. This, monks, is the sixth power of a Tathāgata. Because he possesses this power, he claims his place in the assembly, roars the lion’s roar, and turns the wheel of Brahmā... “Furthermore, monks, a Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes, including one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, many eons of cosmic expansion, many eons of cosmic contraction, and many eons of both expansion and contraction. ‘There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan. Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their aspects and details. This, monks, is the seventh power of a Tathāgata. Because he possesses this power, he claims his place in the assembly, roars the lion’s roar, and turns the wheel of Brahmā... “Furthermore, monks, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, a Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, faring according to their karma. ‘These beings, on account of misconduct in body, speech, and mind, having held wrong views, and having undertaken actions based on wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell. These beings, on account of good conduct in body, speech, and mind, having held right views, and having undertaken actions based on right views, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, faring according to their karma. This, monks, is the eighth power of a Tathāgata. Because he possesses this power, he claims his place in the assembly, roars the lion’s roar, and turns the wheel of Brahmā... “Furthermore, monks, through the destruction of the taints, a Tathāgata realizes for himself in this very life, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having known and realized them through direct knowledge. This, monks, is the tenth power of a Tathāgata. Because he possesses this power, he claims his place in the assembly, roars the lion’s roar, and turns the wheel of Brahmā, which has not been turned by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone else in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. (This concludes the *Daśabalasūtra*, the thirty-fourth discourse in the *Saṃyuktāgama*.)
“A Second Daśabalasūtra,” *Mitteilungen des Instituts für Orientforschung* 6 (1958), pp. 388–392, 395f. [Reprint: Ernst Waldschmidt. *Von Ceylon bis Turfan*.]

The setting was Śrāvastī. Endowed with the ten powers, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, having attained the four grounds of self-confidence, claims the noble, preeminent position of the bull and turns the Brahma-wheel; he roars the true lion’s roar in the assembly.
That is to say: when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises.
That is to say: with ignorance as condition, the volitional formations [arise], up to the point where there is both origination and cessation.
Monks, my Dharma is well-expounded, clear, revealed, with its crossbar shattered, and perfectly proclaimed for gods and humans.

Thus, since my Dharma has been well-expounded, made clear, revealed, with its knots severed, and perfectly illuminated for gods and humans, it is sufficient for a son of good family who has gone forth out of faith to apply himself to yoga;
it is sufficient for him to be heedful.
Enough! One should apply oneself to the teaching of the Teacher.
Let the skin, sinews, and bones remain, and let the flesh and blood of the body dry up;
nevertheless, that which is to be attained by one who has initiated vigor—one who is steadfast, vigorous, and energetic—[must be achieved].
By one of firm prowess who does not cast off the burden regarding wholesome qualities— alas, there shall be no slackening of vigor in the interim before reaching the goal.
For what reason?

The indolent person dwells in suffering, mired in evil and unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by fever, resulting in future suffering, and characterized by birth, old age, and death; moreover, there is a great loss of meaningful purpose.
But the one who has aroused energy dwells in happiness, unmixed with evil and unwholesome states.

Through [these teachings] which lead to affliction, to renewed existence, to feverish distress, and to the ripening of suffering— resulting in birth, old age, and death in the future— the fulfillment of a great purpose is achieved.
This teaching is like a pavilion.
That is to say: the Teacher is present in person, and the Dharma is being taught—which is conducive to peace, leading to final nirvāṇa, resulting in full awakening, and proclaimed by the Sugata.
Therefore, monks, those who regard their own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both, should train themselves in this way:
"May our going forth not be in vain, but fruitful, bringing about happiness and resulting in happiness. For those [who do so]...

"And we shall enjoy their robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; will the services rendered to them indeed result in exceedingly great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great expansion?"— thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Discourse on the Ten Powers (Daśabala-sūtra). It is completed.

The setting was Śrāvastī.

Monks, through revulsion for form, through dispassion toward form, through its cessation, and through liberation by way of non-clinging, one is called a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha.
The same should be said for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
A monk, too, through revulsion for form, through dispassion toward it, and through its cessation, by not grasping, attains liberation; he is called an Arhat liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*).
The same should be said for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

In this regard, monks, what is the distinction, what is the intention, and what is the difference between a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), and an Arhat monk who is liberated by wisdom?

“Venerable sir, all phenomena have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, and the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be well if the Blessed One were to explain this very matter to the monks; having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will retain it.
“In that case, monks, listen and pay close and careful attention; I shall speak.”

Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, having himself realized and fully understood the dharmas among those never heard before, being one who has direct knowledge of the present dharma and has attained supreme awakening, teaches the dharma to his disciples for the sake of awakening in the future.
Namely, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the noble eightfold path.

For in this way, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, is the attainer of the path not yet attained, the proclaimer of the holy life not yet proclaimed; the Tathāgata is the knower of the path, the master of the path, and the teacher of the path.

The proclaimer of the path, the guide upon the path; thereafter, the disciples who are endowed [with these qualities], followers of the path, carrying out the Teacher’s instruction, practicing correctly as they have been taught, become successful and they accomplish the right method,
the Dharma, and the wholesome.
"Monks, this is the distinction, this is the intention, this is the difference between a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, and an Arhat monk who is liberated through wisdom.
(DbSū(3) 12) These five powers of one in training are the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

(DbSū(3) 13) What are the five powers of one in training? They are: the power of faith that is a power of one in training; the power of energy; the power of moral shame; the power of dread of blame; and the power of wisdom that is a power of one in training."
DbSū(3) 14. What are the ten powers of a Tathāgata? Which ten?
DbSū(3) 15.1a Here, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, what is possible as possible, and what is impossible as impossible.
DbSū(3) 15.1b In that the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible—
This is the first power of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one,
claims his noble and preeminent place, turns the Brahma-wheel, and rightly roars the lion’s roar in the assembly.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as they truly are, the undertakings of actions and dharmas— past, future, and present— in terms of their basis, cause, substance, and maturation.

DbSū(3) 15.2b: That the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, past, future, and present undertakings of actions and dharmas—according to their basis, their cause, their object, and their maturation—this is the second power of a Tathāgata, by which power [he acts] as before.

DbSū(3) 15.3a: Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the defilement, purification, establishment, and cleansing of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti).
DbSū(3) 15.3b That which the Tathāgata [possesses], up to this third power of a Tathāgata, by means of which power—as before—[he acts].
DbSū(3) 15.4a Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as it really is, the superior and inferior faculties of other beings.
DbSū(3) 15.4b That which the Tathāgata [possesses] regarding other beings, up to this fourth power of a Tathāgata, by means of which power—as before—[he acts].
Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the various inclinations of other beings.
That the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the various inclinations of other beings—this is the fifth power of a Tathāgata, as described previously.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the world with its various elements and its manifold elements.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the world with its various elements and its manifold elements—this is the sixth power of a Tathāgata, as before.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the path leading everywhere.
That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the path leading everywhere—this is the seventh power of a Tathāgata, as before.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold previous existences, namely: one birth, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many hundreds of thousands of births, and even many eons of world-dissolution.
He recollects even many aeons of evolution, as well as aeons of both dissolution and evolution: "Those beings were named thus;

there I existed, with such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a long life, such a duration, and such a limit to my lifespan. Having passed away from there, I was reborn in that other place."
"From there he passed away and was reborn there; from there he passed away and was reborn here"—thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes, causes, and details.
That the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes—namely, one birth, two, three, and so on as before—this is the eighth power of a Tathāgata.
By that power, as before... Furthermore, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata sees beings—
those passing away and those being reborn, the beautiful and the ugly, the lowly and the exalted.
He knows, as it truly is, that beings go to a good destination or to a miserable destination according to their karma:

"These worthy beings, possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech and mind, revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong views, because of undertaking actions and dharmas based on wrong view— for that cause, for that reason— [go to a state of misery]."
After the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in the hells.

Or again, these beings, friends, are endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view; because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on right view, for that reason—
With that as their condition, after the breaking up of the body, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods.

(DbSū(3) 15.9b) That the Tathāgata, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, sees sentient beings—as described before—this is the ninth power of a Tathāgata, by which power [he acts], as described before. (DbSū(3) 15.10a) Furthermore, through the destruction of the outflows, the Tathāgata attains the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.

Having realized it for himself in this very life, having witnessed it and attained it, he declares: "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further state of existence beyond this.

This is the tenth power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which—due to the destruction of the outflows—as previously described—he [attains] this, which is the tenth power of a Tathāgata, by which power—as previously described—[he acts].
The Blessed One spoke thus; with their minds satisfied, those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The Daśabala-sūtra is completed.

"Having such a long duration of stay and such a limit to my lifespan, having passed away from there, I was reborn there; having passed away from there, I was reborn there; having passed away from there, I have been reborn here"—thus [he remembers] with its specific characteristics, its causal basis, and its detailed description.
He recollects his manifold past abodes. This is the eighth power of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one,
claims the noble place of the bull, turns the Brahma-wheel, and rightly roars the lion’s roar in the assembly.
Furthermore, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn— whether beautiful or ugly, lowly or exalted—
and he understands as it really is how beings fare according to their karma, going to happy destinies or miserable destinies.

Thus, these worthy beings, being possessed of misconduct of body and possessed of misconduct of speech and mind, revilers of the noble ones and holders of wrong views, because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on wrong view— for that cause and by that condition— after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a downfall, in the hells.
Furthermore, these beings, sirs, who are endowed with good conduct of body, and endowed with good conduct of speech and mind;

who do not revile the noble ones; who possess right view; and who, by reason of undertaking actions and dharmas based on right view—on that cause and by that condition—are reborn after the breakup of the body in a happy destination, in the heavenly world, among the gods.
With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses that of humans, the Tathāgata sees beings— those passing away and those being reborn, the beautiful and the ugly, the lowly and the exalted—
and he understands, as it truly is, how beings fare according to their karma, whether they go to a good destination or a bad destination.

Thus, these worthy beings, possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech and mind, revilers of the noble ones, holders of wrong views— on account of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on wrong view, and with that as cause and that as condition, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in the hells.
Furthermore, these beings, sirs, being endowed with good conduct of body, and endowed with good conduct of speech and mind,

not reviling the noble ones, possessing right view, and because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on right view— for that cause and for that condition— upon the dissolution of the body, they are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods.
This is the ninth power of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one,
claims the noble place of the bull, turns the Brahma-wheel, and rightly roars the lion’s roar in the assembly.
Furthermore, through the destruction of the outflows, the Tathāgata possesses the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.

Having realized it for himself in this very life, having witnessed it and attained it, he declares: "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further state of existence beyond this.
This is because the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the outflows, has attained the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.

Having realized it for himself in this very life, having witnessed it and attained it, he declares: "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further state of existence beyond this.
This is the tenth power of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, [is so called].
He claims the noble, bull-like position; he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel and rightly roars the lion’s roar in the assembly.

And if they were to ask that Tathāgata a question regarding the power of knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthānajñānabala*), [they would ask] how that power of knowledge of what is possible and impossible has been known, seen, understood, discerned, and perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
In that way, the Tathāgata, when asked a question, would explain it.
And they might ask the Tathāgata a question regarding the power of knowledge of the ownership of actions (*karmasvakajñānabala*),
such as how that power of knowledge of the ownership of actions is known, seen, understood, cognized, and perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
In that way, the Tathāgata would answer the question when asked.

And they might ask the Tathāgata a question regarding the power of knowledge concerning the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, just as that power of knowledge concerning the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments is known and seen by the Tathāgata.
Having known it, having understood it, and having perfectly awakened to it exactly as it is, the Tathāgata would answer the question when asked.

And if other beings were to ask that Tathāgata about the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties of other beings— just as that power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties of other beings is known by the Tathāgata.
When asked a question, the Tathāgata would answer it exactly as it has been seen, known, understood, and perfectly awakened to. Furthermore,
other beings might ask the Tathāgata a question regarding the power of his knowledge of the various inclinations of other beings,
just as that power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the various inclinations of other beings has been known, seen, understood, and realized by him.
The Tathāgata would answer the question exactly as it was rightly and perfectly awakened to.
And they might ask that Tathāgata a question regarding the power of knowledge of the various elements (*nānādhātujñānabala*),
just as that power of knowledge of the various elements has been known, seen, understood, cognized, and rightly and perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
In that same way, the Tathāgata would answer the question when asked.
And they might ask the Tathāgata a question regarding the power of knowledge of the path leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*),
just as that power of knowledge of the path leading everywhere has been known, seen, understood, and realized by the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata would answer the question exactly as it was rightly and perfectly awakened.
And if they were to ask that Tathāgata a question regarding the power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛtijñānabala*),
he would explain it just as that power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives has been known, seen, understood, and realized by the Tathāgata in its entirety.
In that very way, having perfectly awakened to it, the Tathāgata would answer the question when asked.
And they might ask the Tathāgata a question regarding the power of knowledge of death and rebirth,
just as that power of knowledge of death and rebirth has been known, seen, understood, discerned, and perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
In that same way, the Tathāgata would answer the question when asked.
And they might ask the Tathāgata a question regarding the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*),
[asking] how that power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows has been known, seen, understood, discerned, and perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata.
In that same way, the Tathāgata, when asked a question, would answer it.
(DbSū(4) 7.1) "O monks, I say that the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated.
(DbSū(4) 7.2) O monks, I say that the power of knowing that beings are the owners of their own karma belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated."

"O monks, regarding the power of knowledge of the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, I say it belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated. O monks, regarding the power of knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of other beings, I say it belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated.
O monks, regarding the power of knowledge of the various inclinations of other beings, I say it belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated."
“Monks, regarding the power of knowledge of the diversity of elements, I say it belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated.

Monks, regarding the power of knowledge of the path leading everywhere, I say it belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated. Monks, regarding the power of knowledge of the recollection of past abodes, I say it belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated.”
